summary: This RFC describes the Resource Location Protocol, which lets a host ask on its network where a service or resource can be found. It works best on networks that support broadcast, but can be used elsewhere. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: You shout in a big room, "Who has a printer?" and whoever does shouts back. This is a way for computers to do the same.

questions: what is the resource location protocol
how do hosts find network services by broadcast
how does rlp resource location work
subtitle: A broadcast-based way for computers to find network services.

tldr.problem: Hosts on a network sometimes need to find where a particular service or resource is located, such as a gateway or domain name server, and may not know which hosts provide it.
tldr.mechanism: The Resource Location Protocol uses broadcast or direct requests to ask hosts whether they provide a specific resource, identified by protocol number and optional parameters. Hosts answer if they support the resource.
tldr.outcome: Clients learn the address of a host providing the service they need, without requiring prior knowledge of where it is. This is most effective on networks with broadcast capability.

today: RFC 887 is an Experimental protocol from December 1983 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a resource discovery mechanism for early Internet networks with broadcast capability.

sections.title: Finding Services Without Knowing Where
sections.content:
The Resource Location Protocol (RLP) solves a common problem: a host needs to find where on the network a particular service is provided, but does not know which host offers it. Examples include a newly rebooted host looking for a gateway to reach other networks, or a host needing to find a domain name server to translate hostnames to IP addresses.

Instead of keeping a directory or having a central server, RLP lets hosts broadcast a request: "Who provides X?" Any host that provides the service can respond. This works well on local networks with broadcast support, but the RFC also defines a directed query mode for networks without broadcast.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of having one person who knows everything, everyone just asks out loud who can help with what they need.

sections.title: Naming Resources
sections.content: Resources are named using two parts: a protocol number (the Internet Protocol number for the lowest-level transport) and a resource-specific identifier. For example, the domain name server runs on top of UDP (protocol 17) at port 53, so it is named as protocol 17 with identifier 53. A host looking for just UDP service uses protocol 17 with an empty identifier. This flexible naming allows resources at any protocol layer to be located.
sections.plainLanguage: You describe what you need by saying the type of service and any special details, like the type of phone (landline) and the department (accounting).

sections.title: Four Request Types and Two Reply Types
sections.content:
RLP defines four request message types:

  • Who-Provides?: Broadcast request; hosts reply only if they support the resource.
  • Do-You-Provide?: Directed request; host always replies, even if it does not support the resource.
  • Who-Anywhere-Provides?: Broadcast request for third-party information; hosts may report other hosts that provide the service.
  • Does-Anyone-Provide?: Directed version of the third-party query.

Reply messages are I-Provide (for direct queries about the sender's services) and They-Provide (for third-party information). Each message includes a type byte, flags, a message ID for matching requests to replies, and a resource list.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask everyone on the network, or ask one person directly. You can ask what they have, or ask what other places they know about.

sections.title: How a Lookup Works
sections.content:
When a host needs to locate a resource, it constructs a resource list and sends a request (typically broadcast). Each receiving host checks whether it provides the named resource by examining the protocol number and identifier components in order. If the host provides the resource, it replies with a message listing the resources from the request that it supports, in the same order.

The querying host remembers which peer sent a successful reply, so it knows where to send traffic for that service. The RFC includes detailed examples showing how to find gateways, TFTP-based crash dump servers, and domain name servers, including cases where the querying host must confirm third-party information.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask, wait for answers, and remember who answered. If someone tells you a friend has what you need, you can ask that friend directly to make sure.

sections.title: Network Requirements and Usage
sections.content:
RLP runs on top of UDP (Internet Protocol number 17) and IP, using UDP port 39 (47 octal). It works best on networks with broadcast capability, such as Ethernet. On networks without broadcast, a host can use the directed query types if it knows the address of a resource location server.

The protocol supports a local-only flag that restricts replies to services on the directly connected network, preventing unnecessary replies from distant hosts. The RFC names two major early uses: the Internet Name Server and the Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP).
sections.plainLanguage: This works like talking in a room with your voice carrying to everyone. Some networks do not work that way, so the protocol has a backup mode where you can ask a specific person instead.
